patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Yellow skin, itching and dark urine for 2 weeks, with weight loss

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with painless obstructive jaundice, weight loss and back pain in an older smoker, often with new-onset diabetes or a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign).

points: No abdominal colic; a dull ache going **into his back**.
Lost **9 kg** in 3 months without trying.

steps.lead: Desmond has **painless obstructive jaundice** with weight loss and back pain: the head-of-pancreas picture.
Desmond smokes, is overweight and has **diabetes that started at 67**: late-onset diabetes is a recognised red flag.

visual.title: Where Desmond's ache is
visual.caption: Vague epigastric ache boring into the back: retroperitoneal spread. The jaundice itself is painless.

points: A **smooth, non-tender mass** below the right costal margin.
It moves with breathing: the gallbladder.

steps.lead: Desmond's painless palpable gallbladder with jaundice is **Courvoisier's sign**: a pancreatic head tumour, not stones.

steps.q: Which is the most likely cause of Desmond's jaundice?
steps.r: Painless jaundice, weight loss, new diabetes and **Courvoisier's sign** point to a **pancreatic head** tumour. Stones are painful and the gallbladder is fibrosed.

steps.lead: Most tumours like Desmond's are **ductal adenocarcinomas**, and most arise in the **head**, which is why the bile duct blocks.
Desmond has no **hepatomegaly, ascites or cachexia** yet, which would suggest liver metastases and late disease.

steps.text: **Trousseau's syndrome** (migratory thrombophlebitis, red tender veins in different places) in an older smoker is a pancreatic cancer clue, not a primary clotting disorder.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (pancreatic protocol CT), 'initial investigation' (LFTs, ultrasound), and CA 19-9 as the tumour marker used to monitor disease.

steps.title: Desmond's bloods
steps.text: Cholestatic LFTs (ALP and γGT far higher than ALT), anaemia and hyperglycaemia.

steps.lead: Desmond's first tests fit: **cholestatic LFTs**, high glucose, anaemia, and a very high **CA 19-9**. His ultrasound shows a dilated bile duct.

visual.title: CA 19-9
visual.label: Desmond 1,240
visual.caption: CA 19-9 supports the diagnosis and is used to monitor progression, but it is also raised by cholestasis.

steps.q: Desmond is 68 with weight loss and jaundice. Which scan defines the tumour?
steps.r: **Pancreatic protocol high-resolution CT** is the key diagnostic and staging scan.

steps.lead: Desmond is over 60 with weight loss and back pain, so he needs a **pancreatic protocol CT within 2 weeks**.

points: CT: 3 cm mass in the **pancreatic head**.
Both the CBD and pancreatic duct are dilated: **double duct sign**.
No liver metastases; vessels not encased.

steps.lead: Desmond's CT plus **endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy** confirm and stage his tumour: it looks **resectable**.

steps.title: Investigating painless jaundice
nodes: Pancreatic protocol CT (within 2 weeks if ≥60 + weight loss)
EUS ± biopsy for tissue and staging
steps.caption: Ultrasound first, CT to diagnose and stage, EUS for tissue.

steps.text: CA 19-9 is **not** a screening test: it rises in cholestasis and chronic pancreatitis. Its main use is **monitoring** disease.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' choosing between Whipple's for a resectable head tumour, ERCP and stent for jaundice, pancreatin for steatorrhoea, and FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine for advanced disease.

steps.q: Desmond's head-of-pancreas tumour is resectable. Which operation?
steps.r: Head tumours need a **Whipple** (pancreaticoduodenectomy). Distal pancreatectomy is for body or tail tumours.

steps.lead: Desmond has a **Whipple procedure**, then **adjuvant chemotherapy** (e.g. gemcitabine) to reduce recurrence.
Had Desmond's tumour been locally advanced or metastatic, **FOLFIRINOX** or gemcitabine-based chemotherapy would replace surgery.

steps.title: Pancreatic cancer management
nodes: Resectable head tumour → Whipple + adjuvant gemcitabine

visual.title: Desmond's bilirubin
visual.caption: Bilirubin climbs until an ERCP stent relieves the obstruction, then falls before surgery.

steps.lead: Desmond gets an **ERCP and biliary stent** for his jaundice, **pancreatin** with meals for his pale greasy stools, and analgesia.
If Desmond spikes a **fever** with jaundice and RUQ pain after stenting, it is **cholangitis**: urgent antibiotics and ERCP.

steps.text: Steatorrhoea in pancreatic cancer = not enough lipase reaching the gut. Treat with **pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancreatin)**, not loperamide.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the jaundice is obstructive with pale stools, why steatorrhoea occurs, why the gallbladder is palpable (Courvoisier's law), and why Trousseau's or diabetes appear.

steps.lead: Desmond's tumour grew silently in the **retroperitoneum**, surrounded by **desmoplastic stroma**, and had spread along nerves before he noticed anything.

steps.title: Why Desmond turned yellow
nodes: Tumour in the head of the pancreas
Compresses the distal common bile duct
Conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut
Backs up into blood: jaundice, itch, dark urine
No bile in the gut: pale stools

steps.lead: Desmond's pale greasy stools come from **no bile** and **too little pancreatic lipase** reaching the duodenum.
Desmond's healthy gallbladder could distend behind the blockage. A stone-scarred gallbladder is **fibrotic** and cannot: **Courvoisier's law**.

steps.q: Why does Trousseau's syndrome occur in pancreatic cancer?
steps.r: A **paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state** driven by tumour **tissue factor and mucin**.

steps.lead: Desmond's diabetes 6 months before diagnosis is likely **paraneoplastic**: tumour factors disturbing **islet cell** function.

mcq.q: What is the most common type of pancreatic cancer?
mcq.r: **Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma**, usually in the head.
**Painless palpable gallbladder + jaundice** suggests malignant obstruction.

mcq.q: What is the double duct sign?
Which is a recognised paraneoplastic association?
What is the key diagnostic imaging test?
Which tumour marker is used to monitor pancreatic cancer?
mcq.r: **CA 19-9**; AFP is liver, CA 125 ovary, CEA colorectal.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has painless jaundice and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. A student asks why a gallstone blocking the bile duct would not usually cause the same sign.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Gallstones cause cholangitis that shrinks the duct
Gallstones dissolve before the gallbladder distends
Pancreatic tumours secrete fluid into the gallbladder
Stone-diseased gallbladders are fibrotic and cannot distend
Tumours block the cystic duct directly
practice.e: Courvoisier's law: chronic gallstone disease scars the gallbladder so it cannot distend; a palpable gallbladder in jaundice suggests malignant obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cholangitis does not explain gallbladder size.
Tumours do not secrete into the gallbladder.
The tumour blocks the distal CBD, not the cystic duct.

glossary.pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: The commonest pancreatic cancer, arising from the cells lining the pancreatic ducts.
glossary.head of the pancreas: The part of the pancreas in the curve of the duodenum, next to the bile duct.
glossary.obstructive jaundice: Yellowing from blocked bile flow, with dark urine, pale stools and itch.
glossary.painless jaundice: Jaundice without biliary colic, a classic sign of malignant obstruction.
glossary.pruritus: Itching, caused here by retained bile salts.
glossary.steatorrhoea: Pale, greasy, floating stools from fat malabsorption.
glossary.Courvoisier's sign: A painless palpable gallbladder with jaundice, suggesting malignancy rather than stones.
glossary.Courvoisier's law: In jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to gallstones.
glossary.Trousseau's syndrome: Migratory thrombophlebitis from a cancer-driven hypercoagulable state.
glossary.migratory thrombophlebitis: Inflamed, clotted superficial veins appearing in different places over time.
glossary.double duct sign: Dilation of both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct on imaging.
glossary.paraneoplastic: Caused by substances a tumour releases, not by the tumour's local growth.
glossary.cachexia: Severe wasting of muscle and fat in chronic illness such as cancer.
glossary.ascites: Fluid collecting in the peritoneal cavity.
glossary.CA 19-9: A tumour marker linked to pancreatic cancer, used mainly to monitor disease.
glossary.pancreatic protocol CT: A multiphase CT designed to show the pancreas, tumour and nearby vessels.
glossary.EUS: Endoscopic ultrasound: a scope-mounted ultrasound used to image and biopsy the pancreas.
glossary.endoscopic ultrasound: Ultrasound from inside the gut, allowing pancreatic biopsy.
glossary.Whipple procedure: Pancreaticoduodenectomy: removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, bile duct and gallbladder.
glossary.pancreaticoduodenectomy: The Whipple operation for pancreatic head tumours.
glossary.adjuvant chemotherapy: Chemotherapy given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence.
glossary.gemcitabine: A chemotherapy drug used for pancreatic cancer.
glossary.FOLFIRINOX: Combination chemotherapy (folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, oxaliplatin) for advanced pancreatic cancer.
glossary.biliary stent: A tube placed in the bile duct, usually at ERCP, to relieve obstruction.
glossary.ERCP: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography: endoscopic access to the bile duct for stenting.
glossary.pancreatin: Pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals to treat steatorrhoea.
glossary.pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy: Oral pancreatic enzymes (e.g. pancreatin) to replace missing digestive enzymes.
glossary.faecal elastase: A stool test for pancreatic exocrine function; low means insufficiency.
glossary.desmoplastic stroma: Dense fibrous tissue that surrounds pancreatic tumour cells.
glossary.perineural invasion: Tumour spreading along nerves, causing back pain.
glossary.retroperitoneal: Lying behind the peritoneum, at the back of the abdomen.
glossary.γGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase, a liver enzyme raised with ALP in cholestasis.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase, raised in bile duct obstruction.
glossary.cholestatic: Describing a pattern of reduced bile flow: ALP and γGT raised more than ALT.
glossary.acute cholangitis: Infection of an obstructed bile duct: fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
